sounds.intro: Afrikaans is written in the Latin alphabet with accents on some vowels (ê, ë, ô, ï). It has no genders and almost no verb endings, so it is one of the easiest languages for English speakers. Spelling is quite regular.
rows: a rough sound from the throat, like Scottish "ch" in "loch"
like "ay" with rounded lips, like English "ay-ee" said fast
notes: Double letters (aa, ee, oo, uu) make the vowel long.
Words are often shortened when spoken, for example "dit is" becomes "dis".

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Afrikaans uses the same pronoun for every verb. "Jy" is you, and "u" is the polite you. "Hy" is he, "sy" is she, "dit" is it.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Most nouns add -e or -s in the plural. There are no genders. The word for "the" is always "die".

grammar.title: To be: wees
text: "Wees" (to be) is "is" in the present for everyone, even "ek" and "ons".

grammar.title: Het: have
text: "Het" (to have) is the same for everyone. "Daar is" means "there is".

grammar.title: Present tense
text: There is no ending. The verb stays the same for every person. Werk (to work): ek werk, jy werk, hulle werk.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb is the second item: Ek lees 'n boek. If another word comes first, the verb still stays second: Vandag lees ek 'n boek.

grammar.title: Negation
text: Afrikaans uses two "nie": one after the verb part and one at the end. Ek werk nie. With a longer sentence: Ek praat nie Engels nie.
ex: I do not have a car
ek het nee uh MOH-tuhr nee
he does not work on Sundays
hy werk nie op Sondae nie
hay vairk nee op SON-dah-uh nee

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Put the verb first: Is jy 'n student? A question word goes before the verb: Waar woon jy?

grammar.title: Question words
text: A question word comes first, then the verb.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: The word never changes: my (my), jou (your), sy (his), haar (her), ons (our), julle (your, plural), hulle (their). To like something, use "hou van".

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: Afrikaans uses "jy" with friends and family. "U" is polite and used with older people, in church and in writing. In shops people often use "jy" too.
rows: hoe gaan dit met jou? / hoe gaan dit met u?
hoo khahn dit met yoh / hoo khahn dit met ew

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: "het" + ge- + verb. Ek het gewerk (I worked). Future: "sal" + verb. Ek sal werk (I will work). Some common verbs use a short past: was (was), kon (could).
ex: ons het na die park gegaan
ons het nah dee park khuh-KHAHN

grammar.title: Commands
text: Use the bare verb: kom. Add "asseblief" to be polite. To forbid, use "moenie ... nie".

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Kan (can), moet (must), wil (want). The second verb stays in its basic form and goes to the end of the sentence.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Common words: in (in), op (on), by (at, by), na (to), van (from), met (with), onder (under).
ex: the book is on the table
die boek is op die tafel
dee book is op dee TAH-fuhl
the cat is under the table
die kat is onder die tafel
dee kut is ON-duhr dee TAH-fuhl
the shop is next to the bank
die winkel is langs die bank
dee VING-kuhl is lungs dee bunk
the park is near the station
die park is naby die stasie
dee park is nah-BAY dee STAH-see
the key is in the bag
die sleutel is in die sak
dee SLUH-tuhl is in dee suk

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -er for "more", -ste for "the most": groot, groter, grootste. "Than" is "as". Some are irregular: goed, beter, beste.

grammar.title: Everyday sentences
text: Quick sentences to copy and change.
ex: ons het na die park gegaan
ons het nah dee park khuh-KHAHN
